## Intent
Hypothesis: fusing decide+respawn+render into a single loop with the death verdict kept in registers eliminates intermediate storage and lets compiler auto-vectorization in loop 1 approach the streaming ceiling.

## Layout & approach
The AoS layout packs 68 B/particle across 11 fields. Loop 1 touches only pos+vel (24 of 68 B, 35% hot); loop 2 touches age+color+pos+seed (36 of 68 B, 52% hot). The remaining bytes are dead weight dragged through the line filler in both loops. No intermediate storage is allocated — the death verdict stays in registers, which is the fused approach's premise. The fused loop 2 combines decide, respawn, and render in one pass over the same 68-byte stride, avoiding a second full-array read. At 68 B/p the working set spills L1d at N≈481 and L2 at N≈7710, but since neither loop touches more than 52% of each particle, the effective hot working set is smaller — though the line filler still drags the full 68 bytes per cacheline, capping useful bandwidth at roughly half the raw transfer.

## Cache saturation
The ns/p is remarkably flat across N within each death rate. At q=0.01, cost rises only from 21.6 ns/p (N=320, L1d) to 23.8 ns/p (N=7700, L2 boundary) — a 10% increase across two cache spills. The L1d→L2 transition at N≈481 is invisible; the L2→L3 transition at N≈7700 produces a barely perceptible bump. Even the L3→DRAM spill at N≈250000 adds only ~1.2 ns/p (23.6→25.0). This flatness is diagnostic: the algo is not bandwidth-bound, so cache residency barely matters. The dense grid resolves the transitions but they are non-events. The steepest change is the DRAM regime at N≥370000, where cost climbs from 25.0 to 25.8 ns/p — still under 4%. The death rate, not N, is the dominant axis: q=0.01 to q=0.5 adds ~10 ns/p at every N.

## Bandwidth
Achieved bandwidth peaks at 3.15 GB/s (N=320, q=0.01) — only 25% of the 12.69 GB/s ceiling. The memory floor is 5.359 ns/p; this algo runs at 21.6–25.8 ns/p at q=0.01, meaning 4–5x above the floor. The algo is overwhelmingly frontend-bound: at N=10000, frontend_stall is 67.2% with compute at 32.2% and backend at 0.6%; at N=1000000, frontend remains 70.6% while backend rises modestly to 12.3%. The verdict is frontend/overhead-bound at every regime and death rate, never transitioning to bandwidth-bound. Ratios confirm: vs baseline the algo is 0.92–1.08x — essentially identical to naive scalar at every point. At q=0.01 it is 2.9x slower than the winner at small N, narrowing to 2.4x at DRAM. At q=0.5 the gap compresses to 1.9x — the branchy respawn work is the equalizer, but even there the algo never approaches the winner.

## Assembly
Loop 1 (21 insns/iter) shows genuine partial vectorization: `vmovups` loads 16 bytes of pos, `vmulps`/`vaddps` operate on 4 lanes, `vinsertps` and `vshufps` rearrange components, `vmovlps` writes back 8 bytes. This is component-wise vectorization on stride-68 data — useful but covering only 24 of 68 bytes. Loop 2 (271 insns/iter) is the bottleneck: 32 conditional branches, 12 `cmovae` select-chains for clamped color blending, and 21 byte-granular scatter stores (`movzx` + `add` + `cmp` + `cmovae` + `mov BYTE PTR`). Scalar FP (17 ops) handles float-to-int color conversion via `vcvttss2si`. The byte stores (`mov BYTE PTR [r13+r9*1+0x0],bl`) are the cap: each channel requires a 5-instruction read-modify-write sequence. With 271 insns/iter and only 16 vector instructions in the entire step, the frontend cannot feed the pipeline — hence 67–70% frontend_stall. The `cmovae` chains avoid branch misprediction (branch_flush=0.0%) but the instruction volume itself is the bottleneck.

## Verdict
Refuted — the fused loop 2's 271 insns/iter with 21 byte-granular scatters creates a frontend bottleneck (67–70% frontend_stall) that no cache regime or death rate can overcome. The algo matches naive scalar at every point (0.92–1.08x baseline) and is 2.9x slower than the winner at q=0.01 N=320, narrowing only to 1.9x at q=0.5 where the winner also slows. Loop 1's partial auto-vectorization (`vmulps`/`vaddps` on 24 of 68 bytes) is irrelevant when loop 2 dominates at 13x the instruction count. Achieved bandwidth never exceeds 25% of ceiling (3.15 vs 12.69 GB/s), confirming the algo is instruction-throughput-bound, not memory-bound — the fused scatter's byte-granular writes cannot stream regardless of death rate or cache level.
